AR (n = 1 / n = 2) vs SPCFD:SPX
Parameters:
👁 SPCFD:SPX 7757.64
👁 AR daily (500d) 0.52
👁 AR weekly (52w) 0.39

About this chart

The absorption ratio (AR) measures the fraction of the total variance of a set of asset returns that is explained, or “absorbed”, by a fixed number of eigenvectors of the return covariance matrix. A high value implies the market is tightly coupled (“compact”) and therefore fragile: shocks propagate more quickly and broadly than when markets are loosely linked.

Calculation. Universe: the nine original SPDR Select Sector ETFs (XLK, XLY, XLP, XLE, XLF, XLV, XLI, XLB, XLU; the 1998-listed sectors, excluding the later XLC and XLRE). Daily and weekly returns are aligned to a common calendar (1998-12-22→2026-08-07). For each window we compute the eigen-decomposition of the return covariance matrix and set AR = Σi=1 … k λi / Σi λi. The parameter selector above switches between retaining the top k = 1 eigenvector (n=1) and the top k = 2 eigenvectors (n=2). The daily series uses a rolling 500-bar window; the weekly series uses a rolling 52-bar window. AR is plotted beneath S&P 500 candles (SPCFD:SPX) on a shared time axis. The two panes share crosshairs; the AR axis is fixed to the full range across both parameter settings.

Reference. Mark Kritzman, Yuanzhen Li, Sébastien Page, and Roberto Rigobon, “Principal Components as a Measure of Systemic Risk,” The Journal of Portfolio Management, Summer 2011, 37(4):112–126, doi:10.3905/jpm.2011.37.4.112. The working paper (March 2010) is available on SSRN (No. 1582687).

“Compact markets do not always lead to asset depreciation, but most significant stock market drawdowns have been preceded by spikes in the absorption ratio. This suggests that spikes in the absorption ratio are a near necessary, but not sufficient, condition for market crashes.” — Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon (2011), p. 118
